quiz.q: How is a trait applied to a method in RAML?
quiz.explain: Traits are declared with `traits` in the root and applied with `is`; resource types use `type`; libraries are imported with `uses:`.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between a trait and a resource type?
options: Traits work at method level; resource types are templates up to the resource level
Traits are only for security; resource types for data
Resource types must be published to Exchange
quiz.explain: A trait declares common properties for HTTP methods; a resource type defines common properties of resources.

quiz.q: Which RAML construct can be published to Exchange, versioned and reused across any API specification, but can't be an independent spec?
quiz.explain: Libraries, data types and resource types are reused within one spec; a fragment published to Exchange can be reused in other specs.

quiz.q: A request sends an extra `status` field not defined in the RAML object type. What rejects it?
quiz.explain: By default extra properties are allowed; set `additionalProperties: false` to reject them (`additionalItems: false` for arrays).

quiz.q: `securedBy` is set in the root RAML and also on one resource. Which applies to that resource?
quiz.explain: Root-level `securedBy` applies to all resources, but if both are set, the resource level wins.

options: Connects the app deployed on the runtime to its API Manager asset so policies apply
quiz.explain: The Autodiscovery ID pairs the app with the asset; in Studio it's set on the flow containing the APIkit router, and the asset goes from Unregistered to Active.

quiz.q: What is the difference between an API gateway and an API proxy?
options: A gateway handles one API; a proxy handles many
A gateway is one entry point managing many APIs; a proxy focuses on one API
A proxy routes to nodes; a gateway to load balancers
quiz.explain: 100 APIs → one gateway routes them all; without it you'd need 100 proxies.

quiz.q: Ten partners each need their own credentials so you have more control. Which policy fits?
quiz.explain: Basic Auth uses the same credentials for all consumers; Client ID Enforcement gives each consumer its own client ID and secret (invalid → 401).

quiz.q: The threshold is reached and 10 more requests arrive. Which policy queues them for the next window instead of rejecting them?
quiz.explain: Rate Limiting rejects with 429 straightaway; Spike Control (throttling) queues requests and rejects only if not processed within the retries.

quiz.q: Which OAuth 2.0 grant type fits server-to-server communication with no user involved?
quiz.explain: Client credentials is for server-to-server calls with no resource ownership. Authorization code is for signing up with a third-party app.

quiz.q: Why use the JWT Validation policy rather than validating each token with the authorization server?
options: It verifies the signature locally with a cached JWKS key, skipping a call to the authorization server per request
It doesn't need a token at all
quiz.explain: At 1 lakh requests a day, per-request validation calls are very costly; JWT Validation checks the signature, then the claims.

quiz.q: Which statement about On Error Continue vs On Error Propagate is correct?
options: On Error Continue keeps running the rest of the flow
Both stop the process; Continue sends a success response to the next level, Propagate sends an error
quiz.explain: The instructor corrected the common belief: both stop the flow — the difference is the response to the next level (parent flow or consumer).

quiz.q: A child flow's HTTP Requester fails, and its handler is On Error Continue. What happens in the parent flow?
options: The parent gets an error and stops
The Flow Reference gets a success response, and the parent continues to the next component
The Listener returns its error response
quiz.explain: With On Error Propagate in the child, the parent would get an error instead.

quiz.q: One route of a Scatter-Gather fails (no Try). What happens?
options: The other routes are cancelled immediately
The other routes still complete, then MULE:COMPOSITE_ROUTING is raised and the error propagates
Only the failed route is retried
The failed route's output is null and processing continues
quiz.explain: To continue, wrap each route's components in a Try with On Error Continue.

options: It can call a sub-flow, default timeout 5000 ms
It calls a flow or private flow (not a sub-flow), default timeout 2000 ms
It passes the whole Mule event like Flow Reference
It only works in the Playground
quiz.explain: Parameters: flow name, input, timeout. Unlike Flow Reference, it passes only the given input.

cards.back: **RESTful API Modeling Language** — YAML-based, describes REST APIs: requests, responses, schemas, examples, resources, methods, security schemes. Design Center supports 1.0 and 0.8.

cards.front: Which RAML version is the latest?
cards.back: RAML 1.0 (since about 2015–16); 0.8 is the old one and lacks many 1.0 features.
A method-level reusable component, like a function. Declared with `traits`, applied with `is`.
A template for common properties of resources (descriptions, methods, parameters). Applied with `type`.
A collection of data types, security schemes, traits and resource types. Imported with `uses:`, referenced with dot notation (`lib.traitName`).
A reusable RAML part published to Exchange, versionable, reusable across any API spec — but never an independent API spec.

cards.front: Four benefits of traits, libraries and fragments
cards.back: Readability, reusability, modularity, consistency.
String, Number, Integer, Boolean, Date-Only, Time-Only, DateTime (also array and object). Custom types build on them; imported with `types`, used with `type`.

cards.front: Restrict extra properties in a JSON object
cards.back: `additionalProperties: false` (default true). For arrays: `additionalItems: false`.

cards.front: Restrict the number of properties or items
cards.back: `minProperties` / `maxProperties` for objects; `minItems` / `maxItems` for arrays.

cards.front: How do you define security in RAML?
cards.back: In `securitySchemes`, applied with `securedBy` — at root for all resources, or per resource. Resource level wins.

cards.front: Multiple formats / structures for one request
cards.back: List `application/json` and `application/xml` under `body`; join two JSON types with a pipe: `type: jsonOne | jsonTwo`.
Optional base URL for the API resources; URL = baseUri + resource path. A dummy URL is fine during design; the version (e.g. `v1`) is often included.
Swagger is the old name of OAS (Open API Specification), another REST modeling language. If you haven't used it, say so and that you're ready to learn.

cards.front: Same HTTP method twice on one path?
cards.back: No — a resource can have several different methods but no duplicates. A child path like `/employees/department` can have its own GET.

cards.front: Sharing an API spec for testing
cards.back: Internal: Design Center share. External: mocking service + Postman collection, or publish to Exchange, make it public and share the public portal link.
An Anypoint Platform component to manage the policies, alerts, clients and SLAs of APIs.

Publish spec to Exchange → API Manager: Manage API from Exchange → embedded gateway → ID generated (Unregistered) → Studio global element API Autodiscovery on the APIkit router flow → deploy → Active.
A software layer acting as a single entry point for API calls between clients and backend services: traffic management, security enforcement, request processing, response handling, monitoring.
An intermediary for one API that translates requests, enforces policies and routes traffic.

cards.front: Basic Auth vs. Client ID Enforcement
cards.back: Basic Auth: same username/password for all consumers, less secure. Client ID Enforcement: different client ID/secret per consumer, more control; invalid → 401.
Returns the cached response for the same request instead of calling the end system — for responses that rarely change. Better performance, less load.
Different limits for different consumers — e.g. 500 requests/day for one, 1000 for another.
Rate Limiting rejects at the threshold (429). Throttling queues requests for later windows and rejects only if not processed within the retries.
Open Authorization — an authorization framework, not an authentication protocol. A user lets an app access their resources on another app without sharing credentials.
Client gets a token from the authorization server → sends it as a header to the resource server → resource server validates it with the authorization server → valid proceeds; invalid → 401.
Resource owner (the user), resource server (hosts resources), client (requests access), authorization server (issues tokens).
Client credentials (server-to-server), authorization code (sign up with a third-party app), resource owner password (user's own data on the client's server — less secure).

cards.front: OpenID Token Enforcement vs. OAuth policy
cards.back: OpenID Token Enforcement does authentication + authorization; the OAuth policy does authorization only.
Authentication verifies who you are (comes first); authorization grants what you may do — limited by the **scope**.
The series of steps between the actors to get the token and validate it (redirect, exchange the code for a token, use the token).
JSON Web Token — header.payload.signature, separated by dots.
Component: **Try** scope. Flow: the flow's error handler. Project: **global error handler** (separate XML, set as default in the Configuration global element).

cards.front: How do you manage business errors?
cards.back: Raise them on purpose with **Raise Error** or the **Validation module** (e.g. loan age outside 21–60).

cards.front: Order of handlers in an Error Handler
cards.back: Checked in sequence like a Choice — put **ANY last**, otherwise it catches everything.
A sub-flow has no error handler; use a Try scope inside it (or a private flow). It inherits the parent's handling.

cards.front: Continue after an error in For Each / Parallel For Each / Scatter-Gather
cards.back: Try scope with On Error Continue inside the loop, or wrapping every Scatter-Gather route.
flatten removes the first level of sub-arrays; distinctBy removes duplicates from an array or object; `payload - "name"` removes a key.
`read` parses a string/binary (e.g. `read(payload, "application/json")`); `write` turns a value into a string — e.g. to store JSON in a DB column.
filter: array → array; filterObject: object → object. reduce: `$` item, `$$` accumulator; for computation or array → object.
